metadata.title: Twenty Percent, Or Five
metadata.note: ai-explainer spine. Single primary source: Macnamara, Hambrick & Oswald (2014), 'Deliberate Practice and Performance in Music, Games, Sports, Education, and Professions: A Meta-Analysis', Psychological Science. Every figure read out of the paper itself (local PDF, pdftotext -layout), none from secondary coverage. FRAMEWORK: HOW WAS PRACTICE MEASURED / HOW WAS PERFORMANCE MEASURED / WHAT ABOUT THE REST. Hero is B04, the practice-measurement moderator (20/12/5, Q(2)=16.19, p<.001) together with the paper's own line that the log method presumably yields more valid estimates. B05 is the independent second moderator (26/14/9/8, Q(3)=14.41, p=.002) pointing the same way. B07 carries the limit that cuts against the reel's own framing: between-person variance is not a within-person promise.

render.note: 4K-native sources: Manim at 2160p24, Remotion at scale 2.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — composer, ask lands answered. Speaks the author's name.
beats.narration_text: I'm Uday Sonawane. If you practise an instrument with an app that listens, corrects you in real time and logs every minute, there is a published result about exactly that kind of measurement — and it is not the one the marketing uses.
beats.new_visual_element: Claude composer, the topic question answered

shot.show: the Claude composer with the topic question and its three-line answer

props.command: claude "how much of musical skill does practice time actually explain?"
props.segment: Uday Sonawane · Twenty Percent, Or Five
output: but only 5% when practice was logged
and the logs are the accurate method

beats.role_note: premise — name what the tool actually changes, and which part has evidence attached
beats.narration_text: Start with what an AI practice tool actually does. It gives you more repetitions, because you are not waiting for a weekly lesson. It gives you correctness feedback in the moment — that note was flat, that bar was rushed. And it keeps a log: every minute, timestamped, with no memory in the loop. The first two are good. The third is the interesting one, because a log is an instrument, and somebody has already measured what happens to this question when you use one.
beats.new_visual_element: the three things the tool gives you, the third marked

shot.show: more reps / instant correctness feedback / a log — the log marked
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards in a vertical stack. The first two in soft ink with ticks beside them; the third, 'a log of every minute', in terracotta with a chip reading 'this one is an instrument'. A single line beneath: an instrument can be measured against other instruments.

beats.role_note: PROOF rubric — three questions, AS A STRUCTURE before any figure
beats.narration_text: Three questions to ask of any claim about practice and skill. One: how was practice measured — remembered, or recorded. Two: how was performance measured — by which group somebody belongs to, or by a score. And three: what about the rest — because every one of these results explains part of the variation and leaves the larger part unexplained, and the unexplained part is where people put whatever story they already believed.
beats.new_visual_element: the three questions, as a numbered structure

shot.show: three numbered cards: HOW WAS PRACTICE MEASURED / HOW WAS PERFORMANCE MEASURED / WHAT ABOUT THE REST
shot.visual_intent: Three bordered cards land in a row, one per narration step. The third lands in terracotta — it is the one almost nobody asks — and the rest of the reel is scored against all three.

beats.role_note: the headline figure, with its denominator and the study's scale, cited
beats.narration_text: Here is the headline. A meta-analysis across a hundred and eleven independent samples, a hundred and fifty-seven effect sizes, eleven thousand one hundred and thirty-five people. In music, accumulated deliberate practice correlates with performance at point four six — which is twenty-one percent of the variance between people. That is one of the strongest results in the paper. Games came out at twenty-six percent, sports at eighteen, education at four, and the professions at under one percent and not statistically significant. Music is near the top. Twenty-one percent.
beats.new_visual_element: the music figure and the scale of the evidence

shot.show: 21% of variance in music (r = .46), and the study's scale
shot.visual_intent: A large terracotta figure card reading 21% with 'of the variance in music performance, r = .46' beneath. Beside it, stacked, three small ink cards: 111 samples, 157 effect sizes, 11,135 participants. Citation strip names the meta-analysis.

beats.role_note: HERO BEAT — the practice-measurement moderator, which is the whole reel
beats.narration_text: Now question one. How was the practice measured. The paper tests that directly, and it matters more than the domain does. When practice was recalled in an interview, the effect was twenty percent of the variance. When it was recalled on a questionnaire, twelve. And when it was recorded in a log, as it happened — five. That is a statistically significant difference between methods. And the paper is explicit about which of the three it trusts: the log method, it says, presumably yields more valid estimates than the retrospective methods do. The more accurately you measure practice, the smaller the effect of practice gets.
beats.new_visual_element: the moderator — three methods, three numbers

shot.show: 20% recalled in interview / 12% questionnaire / 5% logged — and which is the accurate one
shot.visual_intent: Three horizontal bars in one group, lengths proportional to 20, 12 and 5 percent, each labelled with its method and its r. The log bar is terracotta and carries a chip reading 'the paper's own preferred method'. Beneath, the moderator test. Citation strip beneath that.

beats.role_note: the second moderator — the same shape, independently
beats.narration_text: And it happens again, on the other axis. Question two: how was performance measured. When performance meant which group you belong to — amateur or professional — practice explained twenty-six percent. Laboratory tasks, fourteen. Expert ratings, nine. And standardised objective scoring — an actual measured score — eight percent. Also statistically significant. Two independent moderators, both pointing the same way: the sharper the instrument, the smaller the effect.

shot.show: 26% group membership / 14% lab tasks / 9% expert ratings / 8% objective score
shot.visual_intent: Four horizontal bars proportional to 26, 14, 9 and 8, labelled with method and r, the objective-scoring bar in terracotta. Beneath, a single line: two moderators, same direction. Citation strip.

beats.role_note: the application — the app IS the log, stated carefully and without overclaim
beats.narration_text: So apply it. An AI practice app is not a person being asked how many hours they put in last year. It is the log. It is the high-fidelity instrument, and the five percent row is the row that describes its own measurements. Which does not mean practice does not work — the paper's conclusion is that deliberate practice is important, but not as important as has been argued. What it means is that if the app shows you a rising hours chart and implies the rest follows, it is making a promise its own kind of data does not support.
beats.new_visual_element: which row the app's own data belongs to

shot.show: the app is the log — so the 5% row is its row, and what that does and does not mean
shot.visual_intent: Left, a bordered card reading 'your app = the log method'. A connector to the right, into a terracotta card holding '5%'. Below both, spanning, a quotation card carrying the paper's conclusion verbatim with attribution. Citation strip.

beats.role_note: the limits — including the one that cuts against my own framing
beats.narration_text: The limits, and the first one cuts against everything I just said. This is variance between people, not a promise about you. Twenty-one percent explained across a population does not mean your next hour buys you twenty-one percent of anything — the within-person question is a different question and this design cannot answer it. It is correlational: nobody randomly assigned ten thousand hours. Studies of experts have restricted range, which pushes correlations down. And the paper does not say the remaining variance is talent. It says it is unexplained. Those are not the same word.
beats.new_visual_element: the four limits, the first one marked

shot.show: between-person not within-person / correlational / range restriction / unexplained is not talent
shot.visual_intent: Four rows, each with a hollow unticked box beside it. The first row is terracotta and carries a chip reading 'this one limits my own argument'. The last row shows the word 'talent' with a cross beside it — beside, never through — and 'unexplained' in ink. Citation strip.

beats.role_note: rubric scored on screen, then both sides — be excited / be sceptical
beats.narration_text: Score it. How was practice measured: in the log, which is the accurate method, and the accurate method gives the smallest number. How was performance measured: the harder the measure, the smaller the effect, twice over. What about the rest: unexplained, and left that way. So be excited that a practice app gives you the most honest practice data anybody studying this has ever had, and that the underlying data set is openly posted. And be sceptical of any hours chart that implies the hours are the answer — on this evidence, for the method your app actually uses, they are about five percent of it.
beats.new_visual_element: the rubric scored, then both sides

shot.show: three questions answered, then be excited / be sceptical
shot.visual_intent: Three ticked rows restating the rubric with its answer. Beneath, two bordered cards side by side: BE EXCITED in ink, BE SCEPTICAL in terracotta, each with two short lines. Citation strip carries the open-data note.

beats.role_note: scaffolded task with a GOOD/BAD discriminator
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Open whatever practice app or tracker you use and find the number it is proudest of. Then ask what that number is a percentage of, and whether anyone has checked it against a score rather than against a category.
